results.prompt: Which part of the CRE Go SDK reference should I look at to verify and parse a report in my workflow?
results.answer:
I have what I need.

For verifying and parsing a report, you'll want the **Core SDK** page of the CRE Go SDK Reference (`docs.chain.link/cre/reference/sdk/overview-go` → Core SDK).

The SDK Reference is broken down into several pages, each corresponding to a core part of the SDK's functionality, and the Core SDK page covers the fundamental building blocks of any workflow, including cre.Handler, cre.Runtime, cre.Promise, report verification (cre.ParseReport), and map iteration helpers cre.OrderedEntries / cre.OrderedEntriesFunc.

So the specific function to look for on that page is **`cre.ParseReport`**, which is the SDK's report verification/parsing entry point. (In the TypeScript SDK, the equivalent lives on the Core page as well, where Report.parse(runtime, rawReport, signatures, reportContext, config) parses a report and verifies signatures, throwing on failure.)

A couple of related pages you may also find useful depending on your workflow:

- **Consensus & Aggregation** — if you're producing the consensus result before generating a report. This section describes how to use aggregators like ConsensusMedianAggregation and ConsensusAggregationFromTags with RunInNodeMode to process and consolidate data from multiple nodes.
- **EVM Client** — if you then need to write the verified report on-chain. This page provides a reference for the evm.Client, the low-level tool for all interactions with EVM-compatible blockchains, including read, write, and utility methods.

**Bottom line:** Go to the **Core SDK** section of the CRE Go SDK Reference and look at **`cre.ParseReport`** for verifying and parsing a report within your workflow.

results.prompt: Using the CRE Go SDK, how do I generate type-safe Go bindings from my contract's ABI?
results.answer:
I have enough authoritative information to answer.

## Generating Type-Safe Go Bindings with the CRE Go SDK

The CRE Go SDK strongly recommends wrapping raw contract calls in a **binding** rather than calling the generic `evm.Client` directly. While you could call the generic evm.Client directly from your main workflow logic, this is not recommended. Doing so would require you to manually handle ABI encoding and decoding for every contract call, leading to code that is hard to read and prone to errors. The recommended pattern is to create a binding: a separate Go package that acts as a type-safe client for your specific smart contract. The binding encapsulates all the low-level encoding/decoding logic, allowing your main workflow to remain clean and focused.

### Step 1: Add your contract's ABI

Place your contract's ABI JSON in your project's ABI directory. Create a new file called Storage.abi in the existing abi directory and add the contract's ABI JSON. By convention this lives under `contracts/evm/src/abi/`.

### Step 2: Run the CRE binding generator

Run the CRE binding generator from your project root. This command will automatically generate type-safe Go bindings for all ABI files in your contracts/evm/src/abi/ directory. It also automatically adds the required evm capability dependency to your go.mod file.

The generator behavior is straightforward: The CRE bindings generator reads all .abi files in your ABI directory and creates corresponding Go packages.

### Step 3: Verify the generated output

The generated bindings will be placed in contracts/evm/src/generated/. For a `Storage` contract, after running the command, you should see two new files in contracts/evm/src/generated/storage/: Storage.go — the main binding that provides a type-safe interface for interacting with your contract, and Storage_mock.go — a mock implementation for testing workflows without deploying contracts.

The generated mock file is especially useful because it lets you test workflow logic without needing a deployed contract on a live chain.

### Programmatic generation (advanced)

The underlying generator is also exposed as a Go function. This project utilizes a forked version of abigen (from go-ethereum) that lets you generate Go bindings for your smart contracts using a custom template. You can call it directly via `bindings.GenerateBindings(...)` from `github.com/smartcontractkit/cre-cli/cmd/generate-bindings/evm`, passing either a combined-JSON path or an ABI path, the Go package name, the type name (for single-ABI mode), and the output file path.

### How the binding is used in your workflow

Once generated, your binding wraps the generic EVM client internally. The evm.Client provides the foundational methods for all onchain interactions. It is highly recommended to wrap its usage in a type-safe "binding" for your specific smart contracts. Your binding will use this generic client internally to handle ABI encoding and decoding, making your workflow code cleaner and safer.

When instantiating the underlying client, you must specify the target chain. To use the client, you must instantiate it with the ChainSelector ID for the blockchain you intend to interact with. For example, using Ethereum Sepolia:

```go
import "github.com/smartcontractkit/cre-sdk-go/capabilities/blockchain/evm"

// Instantiate a client for Ethereum Sepolia
sepoliaClient := &evm.Client{
    ChainSelector: 16015286601757825753, // ethereum-testnet-sepolia
}
```

---

**In short:** drop your `.abi` file into your project's ABI directory, run the CRE binding generator from the project root, and it produces a type-safe Go package (plus a testing mock) under `contracts/evm/src/generated/`. Your workflow code then imports that binding instead of hand-encoding ABI calls. For exact command flags and the latest project layout, refer to the Chainlink CRE "Generating Bindings" guide and the [Part 3: Reading an Onchain Value](https://docs.chain.link/cre/getting-started/part-3-reading-onchain-value-go) tutorial.

results.prompt: CRE Go SDK: which client for offchain API calls vs privacy-preserving requests?
results.answer:
I have enough to answer clearly.

## Short answer

In the CRE Go SDK, use two different clients depending on your needs:

| Use case | Client (Go package) |
|----------|--------------------|
| Standard offchain API calls | **`http.Client`** |
| Privacy-preserving requests | **`confidentialhttp.Client`** |

## Details

**`http.Client` — standard offchain API calls**

The SDK Reference describes the http.Client as the client used for making offchain API requests from individual nodes. The HTTP capability is a decentralized service that allows your workflow to securely interact with any external, offchain API, and when you use the SDK's http.Client to make a request (like a GET or a POST), you are invoking this capability. Under the hood, CRE instructs each node in a dedicated DON to make the same API request, and the nodes' individual responses are then validated through a consensus protocol, which ensures they agree on the result before returning it to your workflow.

**`confidentialhttp.Client` — privacy-preserving requests**

The Confidential HTTP Client provides a reference for the confidentialhttp.Client, used for privacy-preserving API requests with enclave execution and optional response encryption. At the capability level, Confidential HTTP lets you make privacy-preserving API calls with enclave execution, secret injection, and optional response encryption. This ties into Chainlink's confidential/TEE model, where a TEE handler executes in the enclave to securely fetch a secret inside the enclave, execute a capability call from within the enclave, and then returns to the DON for any operations requiring decentralized consensus.

## Important related concept: Runtime vs. NodeRuntime

Because standard offchain API calls can't be automatically guaranteed Byzantine Fault Tolerant, the client you use is paired with the right execution context:

- Runtime ("DON Mode") is passed to your main trigger callback and is used for operations that are already guaranteed to be Byzantine Fault Tolerant (BFT); common use cases include writing transactions to a blockchain with the EVM client or accessing secrets.
- NodeRuntime ("Node Mode") represents an individual node's execution context, used when a BFT guarantee cannot be provided automatically (e.g., calling a third-party API); you tell each node to perform a task on its own, and each node returns its own individual answer, and you are responsible for telling the SDK how to combine them into a single, trusted result by providing a consensus and aggregation algorithm.

So in Go, HTTP requests are typically made inside a node-mode block (`RunInNodeMode`) where you supply a `ConsensusAggregation` (e.g., median aggregation) to reduce the individual node results into one trusted value.

## References
- SDK Reference (Go): docs.chain.link/cre/reference/sdk/overview-go
- The HTTP Capability: docs.chain.link/cre/capabilities/http
- Capabilities Overview: docs.chain.link/cre/capabilities
- Key Terms and Concepts: docs.chain.link/cre/key-terms

results.prompt: I need to combine and consolidate data returned from multiple nodes in my CRE workflow. What does the Go SDK provide for that and where is it documented?
results.answer:
For consolidating data from multiple nodes in a CRE workflow, the Go SDK provides the **Consensus & Aggregation** system, used together with **node mode** execution.

## The core pattern: "map-reduce" across the DON

When your workflow fetches offchain data, each node in the Decentralized Oracle Network (DON) runs the logic independently and may get slightly different results. The SDK reconciles these into one trusted value using a map-reduce style flow:

- **Map** — a function you supply runs on every node independently (each node fetches its own version of the data).
- **Reduce** — a consensus/aggregation algorithm takes all the individual node results and reduces them into a single, agreed-upon outcome.

This is driven by `cre.RunInNodeMode`, which runs your function in "node mode" and then applies an aggregator to combine the per-node outputs. For HTTP work, `http.SendRequest` is a convenient higher-level wrapper around `cre.RunInNodeMode`. When deployed, this is backed by true multi-node Byzantine Fault Tolerant (BFT) consensus across capability operations.

## Aggregators available (Go)

The SDK ships several aggregation strategies you pass into node-mode execution, including:

- **`ConsensusMedianAggregation`** — computes the median of numeric results from all nodes (good for prices and other simple numeric values).
- **`ConsensusIdenticalAggregation`** — requires a Byzantine Quorum of nodes to return the exact same value (useful for things like block hashes; works with primitive types or objects composed entirely of primitives).
- **`ConsensusAggregationFromTags`** / field-based aggregation (`ConsensusAggregationByFields`) — for aggregating complex/struct types field by field.
- Additional strategies such as common-prefix / common-suffix aggregation for array data (e.g., reconciling block-header sequences across forks).

## Where it's documented

1. **SDK Reference: Consensus & Aggregation** — the primary reference describing the aggregators and how they combine node data:
   `https://docs.chain.link/cre/reference/sdk/consensus-ts`

2. **SDK Reference (Go overview)** — entry point that summarizes the Go SDK modules, noting that the Consensus & Aggregation section covers using aggregators like `ConsensusMedianAggregation` and `ConsensusAggregationFromTags` with `RunInNodeMode` to consolidate data from multiple nodes:
   `https://docs.chain.link/cre/reference/sdk/overview-go`

3. **Getting Started, Part 2: Fetching Offchain Data (Go)** — a hands-on walkthrough of the map-reduce pattern with `http.SendRequest` and a consensus algorithm:
   `https://docs.chain.link/cre/getting-started/part-2-fetching-data-go`

4. **Conceptual background** — the "Consensus Computing" concept page and the Capabilities overview explain how BFT consensus underpins all of this.

5. **Go package docs** — the SDK source/API reference on pkg.go.dev:
   `https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/smartcontractkit/cre-sdk-go/cre`

**Suggested starting point:** read the Part 2 Getting Started guide to see the `RunInNodeMode` + `ConsensusMedianAggregation` pattern in a working Go example, then use the Consensus & Aggregation SDK reference to pick the right aggregator for your data type (median for numbers, identical for exact-match values, field-based for structs).

A quick note on sourcing: I pulled these details from Chainlink's official CRE documentation, but I wasn't able to open the Go-specific consensus reference page directly (I hit a search limit). The exact Go function signatures and the full list of aggregators are best confirmed on the consensus reference and pkg.go.dev pages linked above.

results.prompt: Which trigger types are available in the CRE Go SDK and where can I find their config and payload structures?
results.answer:
I was able to locate the relevant Chainlink documentation pages, but the search tool hit a usage limit before I could pull the full page contents. Here's what I can tell you, with the authoritative doc locations so you can verify the exact structures.

## Trigger types in the CRE Go SDK

The CRE (Chainlink Runtime Environment) Go SDK exposes its trigger types under the **SDK Reference: Triggers** section. Based on the Chainlink docs, the main trigger types are:

- **Cron trigger** – fires your workflow on a schedule.
- **HTTP trigger** – invokes your workflow from an HTTP request.
- **EVM / Log trigger** – fires in response to on-chain events (EVM logs).

> Note: I couldn't fetch the full pages to exhaustively confirm every trigger type, so please treat the list above as the commonly documented ones and confirm against the overview page below.

## Where to find config and payload structures

Each trigger's **configuration** (what you set when registering the trigger) and its **payload** (the data your workflow receives when it fires) are documented per-trigger in the SDK reference:

- **Triggers overview (Go):** `https://docs.chain.link/cre/reference/sdk/triggers/overview-go` — the index page listing all available trigger types for the Go SDK.
- **HTTP Trigger (Go):** `https://docs.chain.link/cre/reference/sdk/triggers/http-trigger-go` — shows the HTTP trigger's config and payload.
- **The Trigger Capability (conceptual):** `https://docs.chain.link/cre/capabilities/triggers` — background on how triggers work in CRE.

The per-trigger reference pages (linked from the overview) are where each trigger's **Config** struct and **Payload/Outputs** struct are defined. In practice you'll also find the concrete Go types in the SDK source (the `cre-sdk` Go module), where each trigger package defines its `Config` message and the payload/event type returned to the workflow handler.

**Recommendation:** Start at the **Triggers overview (Go)** page — it enumerates every trigger type available in your SDK version and links directly to each trigger's config and payload definitions. That's the most reliable source since trigger availability can change between SDK releases.
